title: Complex facial lacerations and dog bites
subtitle: Clean, protect the nerves and ducts, align the landmarks

sources.title: Rabies vaccines: WHO position paper, April 2018 (Weekly Epidemiological Record 93(16))

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Human and animal bites: antimicrobial prescribing (NG184)

sources.org: Ali SS et al. World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg 8:239
sources.title: Dog bite injuries to the face: a narrative review of the literature

red_flags.text: Facial weakness with a cheek or preauricular laceration: facial nerve branch division.
Clear fluid from a cheek wound, or a wound crossing the line from tragus to mid upper lip: parotid duct injury.
A laceration at the medial end of either eyelid: lacrimal canalicular injury.
Eyelid laceration with any visual symptom: examine for a globe injury before anything else.
A large facial or neck bite in a small child: airway, haemorrhage and a careful look for further bites.
Any animal bite in a rabies-endemic area, including India: transdermal bites, scratches or licks on broken skin need post-exposure prophylaxis.

do_now.text: Airway and haemorrhage first in extensive face and neck bites.
Wash animal bite wounds immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water, for about 15 minutes.
Start rabies post-exposure prophylaxis according to exposure category: vaccine, plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound for category III exposures.
Dog bite that broke the skin and drew blood: offer antibiotic prophylaxis if it is deep, a puncture, a crush, contaminated or involves deep structures; consider it for any bite to the face.
Check tetanus status and immunise per the national schedule.

assess.text: Test each facial nerve branch before local anaesthetic: forehead, eye closure, smile and lower lip.
Map structures under the wound: parotid duct, canaliculi, eyelid margin, vermilion border, nasal and ear cartilage, eyebrow.
Laceration or tissue loss? Viability of avulsed flaps decides between closure, graft or flap.
Photograph before and after repair. In children, consider safeguarding and the circumstances of the bite.
Most complex facial repairs in young children need general anaesthesia to be done properly.

investigate.text: Facial bone imaging when a fracture is suspected, or a radiograph for a retained tooth fragment.
Swab a wound that is already infected; do not swab a fresh wound routinely.

resuscitate.text: Control bleeding with pressure and sutures under direct vision. Do not clamp blindly in the face, where nerves run with vessels.

definitive.text: After thorough irrigation and minimal debridement, primary closure of facial dog bites is usually appropriate: the facial blood supply tolerates it and the cosmetic outcome is better.
Align landmarks first: vermilion border, eyelid margin, eyebrow (never shaved), alar rim and helical rim. Then close in layers.
Tissue loss: preserve viable tissue and plan graft or flap reconstruction rather than closing under tension.
Complete the rabies vaccine schedule as prescribed, and follow national rabies guidance (in India, the National Rabies Control Programme).
Review the wound early if infection develops, worsens rapidly, or does not improve within 24 to 48 hours.

escalate.text: Facial nerve branch division posterior to the lateral canthus: plastic or maxillofacial surgery for exploration and microsurgical repair early, while the distal branches can still be stimulated.
Parotid duct injury: repair over a stent in theatre.
Extensive tissue loss of the lip, nose, ear or eyelid: specialist reconstruction rather than emergency department closure.

notes: Branches of the facial nerve divided anterior to a vertical line through the lateral canthus are small and usually recover without repair.
The first suture goes at the vermilion border. A 1 mm step there is visible across a room.
Rabies is close to always fatal once symptoms start and entirely preventable before. Wound washing is part of the prophylaxis, not just hygiene.
